say: You give it the **area** formula, $\tfrac12 ab\sin C$. It gives back the **sine rule**, which ties each side to the sine of the angle opposite it.
The key idea: one triangle has one area, however you work it out. Write the area three ways, make them equal, and the sides and sines line up.

example.question: In triangle $ABC$ the sides opposite $A$, $B$ and $C$ are $a$, $b$ and $c$. Using area $=\tfrac12 ab\sin C$, prove that $\dfrac{a}{\sin A}=\dfrac{b}{\sin B}=\dfrac{c}{\sin C}$.

steps.title: Write the area three ways
steps.say: The area formula works from any vertex: take two sides and the angle between them. Do it at $A$, at $B$ and at $C$.

lines.text: All three are the area of the same triangle, so they are equal.

steps.title: Divide by half abc
steps.say: Divide every form of the area by $\tfrac12 abc$. In each one two letters cancel and a single $\sin$ over a side is left.

steps.title: Equate and flip
steps.say: The three areas are equal, so the three results are equal. Turn each fraction upside down to get the form in the tables.

say: You give it a trig equation with $\sin\theta$ and $\cos\theta$ in it, squared as well as to the first power. It finds **every** angle in the range that fits.
Use $\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta=1$ to leave one trig ratio, call it $x$, and the equation is a quadratic in $x$. Solve that, then turn each value back into angles.

steps.title: Leave only sine
steps.say: The equation has $\cos^2\theta$ and $\sin\theta$. Replace $\cos^2\theta$ with $1-\sin^2\theta$ so that only $\hl{1}{\sin\theta}$ is left.

lines.text: Move every term to the right-hand side so the $\sin^2\theta$ term is positive, leaving $0$ on the left; write it with $0$ on the right.

steps.title: Factorise the quadratic
steps.say: This is a quadratic in $\hl{1}{\sin\theta}$. Factorise it, then set each bracket equal to $0$.

steps.title: Find the angles
steps.say: Sine is positive in the first and second quadrants, so $\hl{2}{\frac12}$ gives two angles. $\hl{3}{1}$ gives only $90^\circ$.

lines.text: Both fall inside the range, so keep all three.

say: You give it a **sum or difference** of two sines or cosines, such as $\sin 5x+\sin x$. It gives back a **product** you can factorise or cancel.
Take half the sum of the two angles and half the difference. They become the angles in the product, and the formula tells you which pair of $\sin$ and $\cos$ to use.

how.higher: On Paper 2 it appears once, in 2016, as a 15-mark part where a sum and a difference are turned into products so a common factor cancels.

steps.title: Top line as a product
steps.say: The top is a difference of sines. Use $\sin P-\sin Q = 2\cos\frac{P+Q}{2}\sin\frac{P-Q}{2}$ with $P=7x$ and $Q=x$.

steps.title: Bottom line as a product
steps.say: The bottom is a sum of cosines. Use $\cos P+\cos Q = 2\cos\frac{P+Q}{2}\cos\frac{P-Q}{2}$.

steps.title: Cancel the common factor
steps.say: Both lines contain $2\hl{1}{\cos 4x}$. Cancel it and what is left is $\sin 3x$ over $\cos 3x$.

higher.tip: Write the sum-to-product formula and put the angles in. A formula with some substitution earns low partial credit; a fully substituted one earns high partial credit.

sources.quote: sum to product formula with some
sum to product formula fully substituted

say: You give it one trig ratio of an angle $A$. It finds the ratios of the **double angle** $2A$, or of the half angle.
The formulae come from putting $B=A$ into the compound angle formulae, so $\sin 2A = 2\sin A\cos A$. Find the missing ratio of $A$ first and then substitute.

how.higher: On Paper 2 it shows up in 2016 and 2018 to 2021 and 2023, mostly as a 5 to 10 mark part: proving $\cos 2A=1-2\sin^2 A$, finding $\cos\theta$ from a half angle, or solving $\sin 2t=\sin t$. In 2020 Paper 1 it simplifies an area before differentiating.

example.question: $A$ is an acute angle and $\sin A=\dfrac{5}{13}$. Find the exact value of $\sin 2A$ and of $\cos 2A$.

steps.title: Find cos A
steps.say: The formula for $\sin 2A$ needs $\cos A$ as well. Use $\cos^2A+\sin^2A=1$ to find it.

lines.text: $A$ is acute, so $\cos A$ is positive.

steps.title: Use the sin 2A formula
steps.say: Use $\sin 2A=2\sin A\cos A$ and put in $\hl{1}{\sin A}$ and $\hl{2}{\cos A}$.

steps.title: Use a cos 2A formula
steps.say: You know $\hl{1}{\sin A}$, so use the form $\cos 2A=1-2\sin^2A$.

higher.tip: To prove a double angle formula, start from the compound angle formula and put $B=A$. Writing the formula with some substitution already earns partial credit.
Draw and label a right-angled triangle to get the missing sine or cosine. A relevant labelled diagram earns low partial credit.
When you solve an equation, find every solution in the range. A mark is lost for each solution you leave out.
